items.context: The Transformer encoder is built from a stack of six identical layers. Each layer contains two sub-layers: a multi-head self-attention mechanism and a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network. A residual connection surrounds each sub-layer and is followed by layer normalization. To make these residual connections possible, every sub-layer and the embedding layers produce outputs of dimension 512. The decoder is also a stack of six identical layers, but it inserts a third sub-layer that performs attention over the output of the encoder stack.

items.context: Instead of computing one attention function over vectors of full dimension, the Transformer projects the queries, keys and values several times with different learned linear projections. In the base model h is 8, and each head works with keys and values of dimension 64, which is the model dimension divided by the number of heads. Because each head is smaller, the total computational cost is similar to that of single-head attention with full dimensionality. The outputs of all heads are concatenated and projected once more to produce the final values.

items.context:
Self-attention was compared with recurrent and convolutional layers on three criteria. The first criterion is the total computational complexity per layer. The second is how much computation can be parallelized, measured by the minimum number of sequential operations that are required. The third is the length of the path that signals must travel between two distant positions in the network, since shorter paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn. Learning such dependencies is a key challenge in many sequence transduction tasks, which is why the maximum path length between any two input and output positions is compared for each layer type.

On the second criterion, a self-attention layer connects every position to every other position using a constant number of sequentially executed operations, while a recurrent layer needs a number of sequential operations that grows linearly with the sequence length n. On the first criterion, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers whenever the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimensionality d. This is usually the case for the sentence representations used in machine translation, which are built from word pieces or byte pairs.

For tasks with very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to a neighborhood of size r around each output position. That change would raise the maximum path length to the ratio of n to r, and the authors leave this idea for future work.

Convolutions behave differently. A single convolutional layer with kernel width k smaller than n does not connect all pairs of input and output positions. Connecting them requires a stack of about n divided by k layers when the kernels are contiguous, or a logarithmic number of layers, with base k, when dilated convolutions are used. Either way, the longest paths between positions become longer. Convolutional layers are also generally more expensive than recurrent layers, by a factor of k. Separable convolutions bring the cost down considerably, but even with k equal to n their complexity matches that of a self-attention layer combined with a point-wise feed-forward layer, which is the design the authors chose. As a side benefit, self-attention can make models easier to interpret, because individual attention heads appear to learn different tasks.
items.question: By what factor are convolutional layers more expensive than recurrent layers?

items.context: LoRA keeps the pre-trained weight matrix W0 frozen and represents its update as the product of two small matrices, B and A, so that the adapted weight is W0 plus BA. If W0 has dimensions d by k, then B has dimensions d by r and A has dimensions r by k, where the rank r is much smaller than d and k. Matrix A is initialized with a random Gaussian, while B starts at zero, so the update is exactly nothing at the beginning of training. Only A and B receive gradients.

items.context: Because the update BA can be merged into the frozen weights, LoRA adds no inference latency, unlike adapter layers. On GPT-3 175B, training with LoRA cut the VRAM consumption from 1.2 TB to 350 GB. With a rank of 4 and only the query and value projection matrices adapted, the checkpoint shrank from 350 GB to 35 MB, roughly 10,000 times smaller. A single pre-trained model can then serve many tasks, since switching tasks only requires swapping the small LoRA matrices.

items.context:
LoRA starts from the observation that pre-trained language models have a low intrinsic dimension, meaning that they can still learn efficiently after a random projection to a much smaller subspace. The authors hypothesize that the change in the weights during adaptation also has a low intrinsic rank. For a pre-trained weight matrix W0 of size d by k, the update is therefore written as the product BA, with B of size d by r and A of size r by k, and a rank r far smaller than both d and k. Matrices of this kind exist in every dense layer of the network, so the same reparametrization can be applied to any of them.

During training W0 receives no gradient updates, and both W0 and the product BA are multiplied with the same input, after which their output vectors are summed. The update is also scaled by alpha divided by r, where alpha is a constant. When optimizing with Adam, tuning alpha is roughly the same as tuning the learning rate, so the authors simply set alpha to the first value of r they try and never tune it. This scaling reduces the need to retune hyperparameters when r changes.

The number of trainable parameters follows from the rank and the shapes of the adapted matrices. On GPT-3 175B the authors set a budget of 18 million parameters, roughly 35 MB when stored in half precision, spread over all 96 layers. That budget corresponds to a rank of 8 if one type of attention weight is adapted, or a rank of 4 if two types are adapted. In the comparison that followed, adapting the query and value matrices together gave the best overall results, ahead of adapting a single type of matrix with a larger rank. Surprisingly, a very small rank of one or two already works well, even though the full dimension d of GPT-3 is as high as 12,288. This is why LoRA is efficient in both storage and computation.

LoRA also adds no inference latency. When the model is deployed in production, the product BA can be computed and added to W0 once, so inference runs exactly as in a fully fine-tuned model. Switching to another downstream task only requires subtracting BA and adding a different update, a quick operation with very little memory overhead.
items.question: What parameter budget did the authors set on GPT-3 175B?

The authors note that this benefit lingers even after substantial retraining on the target dataset.

items.context:
Many deep networks trained on natural images learn first-layer features that resemble Gabor filters and color blobs. These features seem not to depend on the dataset or the task, so the authors call them general. In contrast, the features computed by the last layer must depend on the task, because in a network with a softmax output each unit is specific to one class, and the authors call these features specific. The paper measures how features move from general to specific across the layers of a convolutional network trained on ImageNet.

Transferability suffers from two separate problems. The first is the specialization of higher-layer neurons to their original task at the expense of performance on the new one, which was expected. The second is optimization difficulty that appears when a network is split between co-adapted neurons, which was not expected. Depending on whether features are transferred from the bottom, the middle or the top of the network, either of these two issues may dominate.

As a reference point, a network trained on a random subset of 500 classes reaches a top-1 accuracy of 0.625, or 37.5 percent error, which is lower than the 42.5 percent top-1 error of the network trained on all 1000 classes. The error is lower not because the network learned more, but because with only 500 classes there are only half as many ways to make a mistake. The authors also found that transferability decreases as the distance between the base task and the target task increases, yet transferring features even from a distant task can be better than using random features. Finally, they report that initializing a network with transferred features can give a boost to generalization that lingers even after fine-tuning on the target dataset.

A control experiment copies the first n layers of a network, freezes them, reinitializes the upper layers and retrains on the same task. Performance at layers 1 and 2 matched the baseline, but layers 3 to 6, especially layers 4 and 5, did worse. The authors read this drop as evidence of fragile co-adapted features, which interact with each other in a complex way that is hard to relearn.
items.question: What do the authors call the first-layer features that resemble Gabor filters?
